title: The Average Lies
protagonist: Ayo Bankole, financial planner at a credit-union advice desk, with Mara Okafor, an eighth-grader (both fictional)
primary_metric: share of historical windows in which all four tuition bills are paid in full at the gift's size (second axis, declared: share of windows that also leave at least the student's chosen leftover at the end of the last year)

options.A: The Growth Mix — invest the gift mostly in stocks and hold it until the last bill is paid
options.B: The Steady Mix — invest the gift mostly in bonds and hold it until the last bill is paid

scenario_constructions: Ayo Bankole and Mara Okafor are fictional, invented for this case (corpus convention: Rosa Delgado / Fermenter, Dana Osei / The Cold Hit). The gift's size and the number of years until the first bill are scenario constructions; the tuition prices and growth rates are sourced from the College Board's published series at research time; the two mixes are stated rules.
sensitivity_note: Facilitator note (SPEC §6 does not apply as a death/illness stake): family money stress; some students' families carry college debt or have no college fund; students may opt out of the family-money framing and work from the numbers alone. A facilitator-only legal and tax note on gifts to families lives in FACILITATOR.md and not in student text.

deliverables.text: The four tuition bills: the sequence at a student-chosen yearly growth rate within the measured band, the explicit formula for any bill, and their total.

What the calculator says: each mix's compound (geometric) average yearly return beside its arithmetic average, the lump sum a steady-return calculator names (finite geometric series), and a check by writing the steady-return balance recursion and converting it to its explicit form.

What history says: the balance recursion run for every historical window under each mix; the share of windows with all four bills paid, the dollars borrowed in the worst window, and the share that also leave the student's chosen leftover.

The planning gap: for each mix, the smallest lump sum that pays all four bills in at least the share of windows the student chooses, compared with D2's calculator figure in dollars and as a percent, and a two-sentence explanation of why the calculator and history rank the mixes differently.

The order experiment: rerun every failing window with the same yearly returns in reverse order, report how many then pay all four bills as a percent of the failures, and explain in two sentences why a steady average cannot see this.

appendices.title: The Two Mixes and the Counting Rules

balance.argument_a: The Growth Mix produces much more leftover when it works (the grandmother wants leftover for graduate school) and its failures are bounded relative to its upside; at the concept-stage gift it pays all four bills in most historical windows and leaves a substantial amount in about two windows in three (figures to be research-confirmed).
balance.argument_b: The Steady Mix pays all four bills in more windows than the Growth Mix and fails about a quarter as badly when it does; for a family that cannot make up a shortfall, and for a student who cares only about paying the bills, it is the responsible choice (figures to be research-confirmed).
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric: B's share of windows paying all four bills minus A's, as a percent of A's, computed from sourced return series and tuition inputs at the gift's size; second axis (declared so neither option dominates): the share of windows that also leave at least the student's chosen leftover, where A leads for thresholds in the allowed range. Concept stage: about 4.8% on the primary metric.

t4_student_assumptions: The yearly tuition growth rate (D1): the student chooses within the measured 10-year to 20-year band, reruns D3 at both ends, and defends the choice.
The leftover amount worth wanting (D3): the student chooses within the allowed range, or states that only paying the bills matters.
The share of windows required for a plan to count as safe (D4): the student states and defends the reliability level.

Run D1-D2 as a group build, assign D3-D5 as paired work with a shared spreadsheet; one deep-conflict thread instead of two.
No vote; a stated initial position instead; the facilitator plays Mara and asks the three questions from the overview.

real_world_basis.notes: NOT this case's own model data. Real-world context for the facilitator only.
contested_or_overstated_figures_excluded: A widely repeated claim that college prices have risen far faster than inflation for decades is not used; the College Board's own 2025 report shows published public four-year prices rising less than inflation over the last ten years (the case uses current-dollar sticker prices and computes its own growth rates).

Housing, food, books and travel are excluded; the College Board's estimated in-state public four-year budget is $30,990 for 2025-26 (Figure CP-1/CP-9) and none of it beyond tuition and fees is modeled.

context_glossary.desc: The published price of college: the tuition and fees a school lists. Many students pay less after grants and scholarships; that smaller amount is the 'net price'. This case uses the sticker price.

A loan to the U.S. government that pays a fixed rate of interest twice a year until it matures. Strictly, Treasury calls a 10-year security a 'note'; this case uses the market's name, '10-year Treasury bond'.
A stock-market index that tracks about 500 large U.S. companies, weighted by their market value. Buying 'the index' means owning a small slice of all of them at once.

context_why_notes.D1: Why a growing sequence: each year's bill is the last one times a growth factor, so the four bills form a pattern you can write as one formula.
context_why_notes.D2: Why the compound average: it is the steady rate that reproduces what one dollar really became; the ordinary average is higher and would overstate it.
context_why_notes.D3: Why run history year by year: money is paid out as it grows, so the path matters, not just the average.
context_why_notes.D4: Why compare with the calculator: the gap between a steady-return answer and a history-based one is the cost of ignoring risk.
context_why_notes.D5: Why reverse the order: the same returns in a different order change the outcome once money is leaving, which a steady average cannot show.
